item.title: Australia trimmed mean CPI rises to 3.7%, above forecasts, as RBA hike case firms
item.description:
Oil is the clearest driver of the headline beat, and Bullock tied higher energy prices directly to a worse inflation outlook only minutes before the release, so any further rise in crude adds to the case for tightening. The bigger signal for markets is the core reading. A trimmed mean that rose to 3.7%, when the RBA had expected it to stabilise, supports pricing for a hike on November 2 and 3, and backs the Australian dollar and front-end yields. The slightly softer weighted median takes a little off that, but not enough to change the overall message. AUD/NZD traders also face the RBNZ decision at 01:00 GMT, where a widely expected hike could limit any relative move in the Aussie.

---

Earlier:

  • RBA’s Bullock: oil shock means inflation above August forecasts, Board meets next week

---

Australia’s core inflation picked up instead of levelling off, landing just as Governor Bullock was telling senators that inflation is running above the RBA’s forecasts.

Summary:

  • Q3 trimmed mean CPI rose 1.0% q/q (expected 1.0%, prior 0.8%) and 3.7% y/y (expected 3.6%, prior 3.6%).
  • Q3 headline CPI rose 1.3% q/q, above the 1.2% forecast and up from 0.6%.
  • September CPI rose 0.8% m/m (expected 0.7%) and 4.3% y/y (expected 4.2%, prior 4.0%).
  • The monthly trimmed mean rose 0.3% m/m and held at 3.6% y/y, both in line with forecasts.
  • The Q3 weighted median rose 1.0% q/q, slightly below the 1.1% forecast, and 3.6% y/y.
  • The data came as Bullock said inflation will likely exceed the RBA’s August forecasts. The Board meets on November 2 and 3.

Australia’s underlying inflation rose more than expected in the September quarter, with the Reserve Bank of Australia’s preferred trimmed mean measure climbing to 3.7% year on year, strengthening the case for another rate hike when the RBA Board meets on November 2 and 3.

The trimmed mean, which strips out the largest price rises and falls to show the core trend, rose 1.0% in the quarter, in line with forecasts and up from 0.8% in the June quarter. The annual rate of 3.7% was above both the 3.6% expected and the June quarter’s 3.6%. The quarterly pace also ran ahead of the roughly 0.8% implied by the RBA’s August forecasts. Headline CPI rose 1.3% in the quarter, above the 1.2% forecast and more than double the 0.6% rise in the June quarter.

The monthly figures pointed in the same direction. Headline CPI rose 0.8% in September, above the 0.7% forecast, lifting annual inflation to 4.3% from 4.0% and above expectations of 4.2%. The monthly trimmed mean rose 0.3%, in line with forecasts, holding at 3.6% year on year. The weighted median, another underlying measure, was a little softer, rising 1.0% in the quarter against a forecast of 1.1%.

The data landed while RBA Governor Michele Bullock was appearing before a Senate committee. In her opening statement, delivered shortly before the release, she said inflation was likely to run higher than the RBA’s August base case, as the re-escalating Middle East conflict has pushed energy prices well above earlier assumptions and the labour market appears a little tighter than previously judged. She said a key question for next week’s meeting is whether the tightening delivered so far, 100 basis points this year, will be enough to bring inflation back to target in a reasonable time.

Today’s figures add weight to that concern. The RBA still uses the quarterly trimmed mean as its main gauge of underlying inflation, and a rise in the annual rate, rather than the stabilisation the central bank had forecast, suggests price pressures are broadening beyond fuel. Higher energy costs are lifting headline inflation directly, while the firmer core reading points to the domestic capacity pressures Bullock highlighted.

The RBA will publish updated forecasts alongside its decision next week, which will show how far it has revised its inflation outlook and whether it sees the need for further tightening. 

---

item.title: RBA’s Bullock: oil shock means inflation above August forecasts, Board meets next week
item.description:
Oil leads the hawkish read. Bullock tied the deterioration in the inflation outlook directly to re-escalating Middle East conflict and higher energy prices, so further gains in crude feed straight into the case for another RBA hike. By saying inflation will likely exceed the August base case, and asking openly whether current tightening is enough, she leaves the November 2 and 3 meeting live and supports the Australian dollar and front-end yields. Her view that the labour market is tighter than judged, despite unemployment rising, weakens the dovish argument that slowing growth will do the work. Today’s quarterly trimmed mean now becomes the decisive test: a firm print would likely push markets further toward a November hike.

---

Ahead:

  • Australia CPI preview: banks see 1.0% core rise, above the RBA’s 0.8% forecast
  • Economic and event calendar in Asia Wednesday, October 28, 2026. AUD CPI, RBA and RBNZ
  • Australia CPI explained: why 2 inflation readings land today and which one the RBA watches

--- Bullock told senators that oil, AI-driven cost pressures and a tighter-than-thought labour market have pushed inflation above the RBA’s August track, making next week’s meeting a genuine question of whether 100bp of hikes is enough.

Summary:

  • RBA Governor Michele Bullock said inflation will likely be higher than the RBA’s August base case, as some of the upside risks it flagged have materialised.
  • Re-escalating Middle East conflict has pushed global energy prices well above August assumptions, which will add materially to inflation directly and through pass-through of transport costs. Short-term inflation expectations are elevated.
  • She said the labour market looks a little tighter than previously judged, despite unemployment rising more than expected, with elevated underlying inflation tied to domestic demand.
  • Weak productivity growth means a further period of subdued demand growth is needed to bring inflation down sustainably.
  • The cash rate is up 100bp this year. The Board meets next week, with a key question being whether tightening to date is enough to return inflation to target in a reasonable time.
  • Housing prices have fallen in most capitals but remain around 50% above early 2020 levels. Bullock said the RBA does not target house prices.

Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Michele Bullock said inflation is likely to run higher than the central bank forecast in August, as a renewed surge in energy prices from the Middle East conflict compounds domestic capacity pressures, signalling an open question over further tightening when the RBA Board meets next week.

In her opening statement to the Senate Economics Legislation Committee on Wednesday, delivered shortly before the release of September quarter CPI data, Bullock said some of the upside risks to inflation that the RBA had flagged in August have materialised or are materialising. The RBA’s August forecasts had inflation returning to around the midpoint of its 2% to 3% target only in late 2027.

Energy is the main new source of pressure. Bullock said the conflict in the Middle East has re-escalated and global energy prices are now much higher than assumed in August. She said higher oil and related prices will add materially to inflation, both directly and as businesses facing higher transport costs try to pass them on, and noted that short-term inflation expectations are elevated. She also pointed to the global AI boom and extreme weather as sources of upward pressure on technology and agricultural prices.

Bullock stressed that inflation is not only being imported. Even though unemployment has risen a little more than expected, she said the labour market appears slightly tighter than the RBA had judged, citing elevated underlying inflation in areas that reflect domestic demand. Weak productivity growth means the economy cannot grow strongly without adding to price pressures, a challenge she described as fundamental for Australia and for real spending power over the next few years. She said a further period of subdued growth in aggregate demand is needed to bring inflation down sustainably.

The Board has raised the cash rate by 25 basis points since the committee’s June hearing, taking the cumulative increase this year to 100 basis points. Bullock said the full effects have yet to be felt, with household spending moderating only gradually and business investment picking up strongly on data centres and renewable energy projects. Housing prices have fallen in most capital cities, though they remain around 50% above early 2020 levels, and she said the RBA does not target house prices.

Looking ahead, Bullock said the Board will assess the data and the balance of risks next week, with a key question being whether the tightening so far will be enough to return inflation to target in a reasonable time. She added that higher rates are difficult for households but that high inflation cannot be allowed to persist, noting that central banks in many advanced economies are raising rates or signalling they will if needed. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6734 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: HBM explained: the AI memory behind SK Hynix’s record profits and rising chip prices
item.description:
HBM helps explain why the memory upcycle has been so strong. Because it absorbs production capacity, AI demand lifts prices across the whole DRAM market, not just at the high end, which supports earnings at SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron and weighs on margins for PC, phone and server makers that buy memory. The concentration of supply makes the Kospi and the wider Korean market unusually sensitive to AI spending, and changes in HBM market share between SK Hynix and Samsung can move both stocks sharply. The main risk is the cycle turning: if new capacity and three-way competition in HBM4 catch up with demand, pricing power could fade quickly, as it has in past memory cycles.

---

Earlier, stunning results:

  • SK Hynix Q3 operating profit beats at 83tn won, unveils 100tn won shareholder payout plan

--- HBM is the memory that keeps AI chips fed with data, and because it eats so much production capacity, it is pushing up prices for nearly every memory chip in the world.

Summary:

  • HBM stacks thin DRAM dies vertically and places them right next to the processor, delivering much higher bandwidth with less power.
  • AI chips are often limited by how fast they can be fed data, so every leading AI accelerator, including Nvidia’s GPUs, uses HBM.
  • HBM uses around three times the wafer capacity per bit of standard DRAM, by industry estimates, so shifting production to it squeezes supply of ordinary memory and lifts prices.
  • Only SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron make it at scale. Counterpoint puts SK Hynix at around 50% of HBM revenue in Q2 2026, down from around 64% a year earlier, with Samsung at around 33%.
  • All three are in production of HBM4 for Nvidia’s Vera Rubin. Analysts estimate SK Hynix supplies the majority, though Nvidia has not disclosed a split.
  • The risks to watch are new capacity, competition and a potential softening in HBM prices once supply catches up.

SK Hynix’s latest results put a striking number on the AI boom: third-quarter operating profit of around 83 trillion won, roughly seven times the level of a year earlier, on an operating margin of around 80%. The company’s headline figures talk about DRAM and NAND prices, but the product behind much of that surge is high-bandwidth memory, or HBM. Here is what it is and why it matters for markets.

HBM is a type of DRAM, the working memory that holds data while a processor uses it. Ordinary DRAM sits on separate modules some distance from the chip it serves. HBM instead stacks a dozen or more thin memory dies on top of each other and places the stack right beside the processor, connected by thousands of tiny vertical links. The result is a very wide, very short path for data, which delivers far more bandwidth, meaning more data moved per second, while using less power.

That matters because AI chips are often limited less by how fast they can calculate than by how quickly they can be fed data. Training and running large AI models means shuttling enormous amounts of information in and out of memory, and without enough bandwidth, an expensive processor sits idle. That is why every leading AI accelerator, including Nvidia’s GPUs, is packaged with HBM, and why the memory has become one of the most valuable components in an AI server.

HBM also explains why prices for ordinary memory are rising. Making HBM uses far more wafer capacity per unit of memory than standard DRAM, with industry estimates commonly putting it at around three times as much, because the dies are larger, the stacking process is complex and some output is lost along the way. As manufacturers shift production lines toward HBM to meet AI demand, less capacity is left for the conventional DRAM used in PCs, phones and servers. That squeeze helps explain why SK Hynix reported DRAM selling prices up by a high-20% rate in a single quarter.

Only three companies make HBM at scale: SK Hynix, Samsung Electronics and Micron. SK Hynix established an early lead and still holds the largest share, but competition is intensifying. According to Counterpoint Research, SK Hynix’s share of HBM revenue fell to around 50% in the second quarter of 2026 from around 64% a year earlier, while Samsung’s rose to around 33% as it caught up on the previous generation, known as HBM3E. Micron held around 18%. 

The next battleground is HBM4, which doubles the width of the connection to the processor and is being built into Nvidia’s new Vera Rubin platform. Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang said in June that all three suppliers are in production for Vera Rubin, with the first systems due to ship in the third quarter. Analysts estimate SK Hynix supplies the majority of that HBM4 volume, although Nvidia has not disclosed any split.

For investors, HBM sits at the centre of several big questions. It is a key reason memory makers are earning record profits and returning cash to shareholders, but it is also a cyclical business. Some forecasters warn that HBM prices could soften once competition and new capacity catch up with demand. The things to watch are HBM4 volumes and pricing, how quickly Samsung and Micron gain ground, and whether AI spending keeps growing fast enough to absorb new supply. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: SK Hynix Q3 operating profit beats at 83tn won, unveils 100tn won shareholder payout plan
item.description:
The operating beat and a shareholder return of about 100 trillion won give the stock strong support, and the buyback and cancellation of more than 60 trillion won stands out as a structural tailwind for SK Hynix shares and the Kospi, where it is a heavyweight. The net profit miss is the main source of headline risk until the cause is clear. The price data is the bigger signal for the sector: DRAM up by a high-20% rate in a single quarter, together with a 2027 demand outlook of around 25% growth, supports the memory upcycle for Samsung Electronics and Micron. It also confirms that AI infrastructure spending is still feeding through to component costs, which matters for hyperscaler capex budgets and the heavy AI-related debt issuance flagged by Fitch and S&P this week.

---

--- Soaring memory prices drove an operating profit beat at SK Hynix, and the chipmaker is handing back about 100 trillion won to shareholders this year, even as net profit came in well short.

Summary:

  • SK Hynix Q3 operating profit was around 83 trillion won, beating the LSEG SmartEstimate of around 77 trillion won. Revenue was around 105 trillion won against around 98 trillion expected.
  • Net profit was around 40 trillion won, well below the estimate of around 55 trillion won.
  • DRAM average selling prices rose by a high-20% rate from Q2, and NAND prices by a mid-20% rate.
  • The company plans about 100 trillion won in 2026 shareholder returns: more than 30 trillion won in cash dividends and more than 60 trillion won in share buybacks and cancellations, including a newly approved 20 trillion won buyback.
  • The Q3 dividend is 20,000 won per share, including a 10,000 won special dividend linked to its Kioxia investment.
  • SK Hynix expects 2027 DRAM demand to grow by a mid-20% rate and NAND demand by a high-teens rate.

SK Hynix posted third-quarter operating profit of around 83 trillion won, comfortably ahead of expectations, as surging memory chip prices lifted revenue, and the South Korean chipmaker unveiled shareholder returns of about 100 trillion won for 2026, although net profit fell well short of forecasts.

Operating profit came in at around 83 trillion won against an LSEG SmartEstimate of around 77 trillion won, while revenue reached around 105 trillion won, above the roughly 98 trillion won expected. Net profit, however, was around 40 trillion won, far below the estimate of around 55 trillion won. The company’s headline figures did not explain the gap between its strong operating result and the bottom line.

Pricing drove the beat. SK Hynix said the average selling price of its DRAM, the memory used in servers, PCs and AI accelerators, rose by a high-20% rate compared with the second quarter, while NAND flash prices, used in storage, rose by a mid-20% rate. The gains reflect tight supply across the memory market as demand from AI data centres continues to absorb capacity.

The company also set out a substantial capital return programme. It plans shareholder returns of about 100 trillion won in 2026, made up of cash dividends of more than 30 trillion won and the buyback and cancellation of more than 60 trillion won of its own shares. As part of that, it approved a share buyback worth 20 trillion won. SK Hynix declared a third-quarter dividend of 20,000 won per share, which includes a special dividend of 10,000 won per share linked to its investment in Japanese memory maker Kioxia.

Looking ahead, SK Hynix expects global demand for DRAM to grow by a mid-20% rate in 2027 from this year and NAND demand to rise by a high-teens rate, pointing to a further year of strong growth in the memory cycle.

The results reinforce SK Hynix’s position as one of the main beneficiaries of AI-related spending, with the scale of its buyback and dividend plans signalling confidence in cash generation. Investors are likely to focus next on what drove the net profit shortfall and on whether price gains of this size can be sustained into 2027 as new capacity comes online. 

---

SK Hynix is one of the world’s two largest memory chipmakers, alongside Samsung Electronics, and makes DRAM and NAND flash for servers, PCs, smartphones and data centres. Based in Icheon, South Korea, the company began as Hyundai Electronics’ semiconductor arm, was later spun out as Hynix and became part of the SK Group conglomerate in 2012, when SK Telecom acquired a controlling stake. It has become a leading supplier of high-bandwidth memory, the stacked DRAM used alongside AI processors, and counts Nvidia among its key customers. That has made it one of the biggest beneficiaries of the global AI build-out and one of the heaviest-weighted stocks on the Kospi. SK Hynix also holds an indirect stake in Japanese memory maker Kioxia through a Bain Capital-led consortium, which is the investment behind this quarter’s special dividend. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Australia CPI explained: why 2 inflation readings land today and which one the RBA watches
item.description:
For the Australian dollar and front-end yields, the reaction is likely to hinge on the quarterly trimmed mean, not the headline monthly print. A reading at or above the expected 1.0% in the quarter would run ahead of the pace implied by the RBA’s August forecasts and strengthen the case for a hike at the November 2 and 3 meeting. A softer core reading would give the RBA room to wait, even if fuel-driven headline inflation runs hot. A gap between the monthly and quarterly headline figures can trigger an early reaction that later reverses, as traders look past the headline to the core numbers. Oil remains the main driver of headline inflation, so energy prices will shape how hot the monthly figure runs in the months ahead.

---

Earlier:

  • Australia CPI preview: banks see 1.0% core rise, above the RBA’s 0.8% forecast
  • Economic and event calendar in Asia Wednesday, October 28, 2026. AUD CPI, RBA and RBNZ

---

Australia’s monthly CPI now sets the headline, but the quarterly trimmed mean is still the number the RBA trusts most, and that makes it today’s main event.

Summary:

  • Both the September monthly CPI and the September quarter CPI are due at 00:30 GMT (20:30 US Eastern on Tuesday, 11:30 Sydney).
  • Since November 2025, the ABS has published a complete monthly CPI covering most of the basket every month, replacing the partial Monthly CPI Indicator.
  • The monthly CPI is now the headline inflation measure and the benchmark for the RBA’s 2% to 3% target. The quarterly CPI is now the average of its three months.
  • The RBA still uses the quarterly trimmed mean as its main underlying inflation gauge, while watching the newer monthly measures as their seasonal patterns settle.
  • Major banks expect quarterly trimmed mean of around 1.0% q/q and 3.6% y/y, above the roughly 0.8% pace implied by the RBA’s August forecasts. Headline is seen at around 1.3% q/q and 3.9% y/y.
  • The September monthly headline is expected to rise to around 4.2% y/y. It can run above the quarterly rate when inflation is building through the quarter.

Australia releases two inflation readings today, the September monthly CPI and the September quarter CPI, and understanding the difference between them is key to reading the market reaction. Both are due from the Australian Bureau of Statistics at 00:30 GMT, which is 20:30 US Eastern on Tuesday and 11:30 in Sydney.

Until late 2025, the quarterly CPI was Australia’s official inflation measure, and the monthly figure was only an indicator. That old Monthly CPI Indicator updated prices for only about half of the basket each month, with many services priced just once a quarter, so it was patchy and prone to swings. Markets watched it, but the Reserve Bank of Australia treated it as a rough guide.

That changed in November 2025, when the ABS began publishing a complete monthly CPI, starting with October 2025 data. It now collects prices for most goods and services every month, using sources such as web-scraped online prices, transaction records and government data, and it is published with seasonal adjustment. The monthly CPI is now the main measure of headline inflation, and its annual rate is the benchmark against the RBA’s 2% to 3% target.

The quarterly CPI has not disappeared. It is now built from the monthly data, with each quarter’s index the average of its three months, and published alongside the monthly figures in the March, June, September and December releases. So the quarterly headline has largely been replaced in importance, but it is now a by-product of the monthly series, not a separate survey.

The bigger reason the quarterly release still matters is underlying inflation. The RBA’s preferred gauge has long been the quarterly trimmed mean, which strips out the largest price rises and falls each quarter to show the core trend. The central bank still uses that quarterly measure as its main underlying gauge, and its forecasts are framed in quarterly trimmed mean terms, while it watches the newer monthly measures alongside it. The monthly trimmed mean has only around 18 months of history, and its seasonal patterns are still being established, so it can be noisier. The RBA plans to shift toward monthly measures as they bed in, with the ABS committed to producing the quarterly series until at least 2027.

That makes today’s quarterly trimmed mean the number most likely to move markets and shape the RBA’s November 2 and 3 meeting. Australia’s major banks broadly expect it to rise around 1.0% in the quarter and around 3.6% year on year, above the roughly 0.8% quarterly pace implied by the RBA’s August forecasts. On the headline side, quarterly CPI is seen up around 1.3% in the quarter and 3.9% year on year, while the September monthly figure is expected to rise to around 4.2% from 4.0%.

Those two headline numbers are not contradictory. The monthly figure compares September with September last year, while the quarterly figure compares the average of July, August and September with the same three months a year earlier. If inflation is rising through the quarter, the monthly rate will run above the quarterly one, which is what forecasters expect today.

For traders, the practical rule is that the monthly headline sets the tone, but the quarterly trimmed mean carries the most weight for the RBA, at least until the monthly measures earn the same trust. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BlackRock sees one more Fed hike this year, calls market pricing for more too hawkish
item.description:
BlackRock’s view supports the front end of the Treasury curve. If the Fed sounds less aggressive than markets fear this week, two-year yields have the most room to fall, which would steepen the curve. Its caution on the long end, where it still sees yields rising as competition for capital intensifies, matches the heavy-supply theme flagged this week by Fitch and S&P. Neutral positioning on US equities, with a continued tilt to AI and tech, suggests BlackRock expects volatility around policy, not a broad selloff. A dovish-leaning Fed would also cap the dollar. Higher oil remains the main risk to the “less hawkish than priced” view, since further energy-driven inflation would test it.

---

Earlier:

  • FOMC Preview: A hawkish hold as markets watch for signals about timing and extent of further tightening

---

BlackRock thinks the Fed will hike once more and then stop, and it is positioning for that by owning short-dated Treasuries while staying wary of long bonds.

Summary:

  • BlackRock expects one more Fed rate hike by year-end but sees market pricing for further tightening as overly hawkish.
  • It says the recent tightening is not the start of a new, sustained hiking cycle, even after a hotter September CPI showed broadening price pressures.
  • Markets have partly scaled back hike expectations since the September meeting, moving closer to BlackRock’s view.
  • BlackRock is overweight short-dated US Treasuries, favouring the front end for income and a greater breakeven buffer.
  • It is neutral on long-dated Treasuries and still sees room for yields to rise as competition for capital intensifies.
  • It is neutral on US equities, citing strong AI fundamentals but near-term policy volatility, and continues to favour AI and tech.

BlackRock expects the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates once more by the end of the year but sees market pricing for further tightening as overly hawkish, a view that underpins its preference for short-dated US Treasuries over longer bonds, according to the BlackRock Investment Institute’s weekly commentary.

The Fed’s policy decision this week, its second-to-last meeting of 2026, takes centre stage after a hotter-than-expected September CPI report that showed price pressures broadening. Even so, BlackRock said it does not view the recent tightening as the start of a new, sustained hiking cycle. It noted that markets have partly scaled back expectations for further hikes since the Fed’s September meeting, moving closer to its own view, though it still regards the remaining pricing as excessive.

That stance shapes BlackRock’s fixed income positioning. The asset manager is overweight short-dated US Treasuries, saying much of the repricing it had anticipated has already taken place and that expectations for further Fed hikes look too high. It favours the front end of the curve for attractive income and a greater breakeven buffer, meaning yields are high enough to absorb some further rise in rates before investors start losing money.

BlackRock is neutral on long-dated Treasuries. It said higher yields offer attractive income and a bigger cushion against further rate increases, but it still sees room for long-term yields to rise as competition for capital intensifies, a pressure that comes as governments and companies, including those investing in AI infrastructure, borrow heavily.

On equities, BlackRock is neutral on US stocks overall. It said strong AI fundamentals remain supportive, but policy uncertainty could fuel volatility in the near term. Within the market, it continues to favour AI and technology.

Taken together, BlackRock’s positioning amounts to a bet that the Fed will tighten less than markets expect, while acknowledging that the long end of the curve remains vulnerable to supply pressure and that equity gains may depend increasingly on the AI theme. The Fed’s statement and any guidance on the pace of further hikes will be the first test of that view.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: MUFG sees RBNZ hiking to 3% today but under-delivering on pricing, flags NZD downside
item.description:

Neutral or “wait and see” language could trigger a repricing of the roughly three and a half further hikes priced, pulling front-end yields lower and weighing on the kiwi, with AUD/NZD a likely beneficiary ahead of the RBA meeting on November 2 and 3. MUFG thinks the RBNZ will hike today and then disappoint, arguing that New Zealand’s spare capacity cannot justify the rate path markets have priced, which leaves the kiwi’s recent strength on borrowed time.

Summary:

MUFG expects the Reserve Bank of New Zealand to raise its official cash rate by 25 basis points today but to fall short of the hawkish path markets have priced, leaving the New Zealand dollar exposed to downside risk, according to a preview from the bank.

The decision is due at 01:00 GMT on Wednesday, which is 21:00 US Eastern on Tuesday. MUFG said the rates market is almost fully priced for a 25 basis point hike, which would take the OCR to 3% and mark a third consecutive increase. The bank expects the RBNZ to deliver that move, but sees only one further hike after today, to a peak of 3.25%. By MUFG’s reckoning, market pricing implies around three and a half additional hikes beyond today’s decision, with three hikes in total priced by March.

The gap matters for the currency. MUFG noted that the New Zealand dollar has been the third-best performing G10 currency this month, a run it said depends on the RBNZ delivering a hawkish hike and guidance strong enough to validate current pricing. Without that, the support from rate expectations could fade.

MUFG’s case for a shallower path rests on the domestic economy. It said third-quarter inflation came in slightly weaker than expected, which it believes reflects the degree of spare capacity, or unused resources, in the New Zealand economy. The bank also pointed to the jump in the unemployment rate to 5.6% in the second quarter, the highest since the third quarter of 2015. In MUFG’s view, that slack means the economy will not require as much tightening as markets are pricing.

The bank said the risks for the New Zealand dollar are skewed to the downside. Even if the RBNZ delivers a hawkish hike today, MUFG expects investors to question at some point how many increases are priced, and it forecasts the currency to underperform over its forecast horizon.

MUFG’s view puts it at the dovish end of expectations. Locally, ANZ has pencilled in a pause in December, while ASB and Westpac expect the OCR to reach 3.5% by February. All five of New Zealand’s major banks expect the Reserve Bank of New Zealand to raise the official cash rate by 25 basis points to 3% today, which would be its third consecutive hike, but they are divided on how much further the central bank will need to go.

The decision is due at 14:00 New Zealand time, which is 01:00 GMT on Wednesday and 21:00 US Eastern on Tuesday. Markets have roughly 90% of a hike priced in, according to ASB, and BNZ said a decision to hold would come as a material shock.

The consensus has firmed over the past week. Before the September quarter CPI release, Westpac was the outlier calling for a pause, but it now expects a hike today. Kiwibank, which said in September the economy looked too weak for further tightening, also expects a move, though it sees the RBNZ pairing the hike with “wait and see” language before holding.

The banks’ rate paths diverge after today. ANZ has lightly pencilled in a pause in December, with chief economist Sharon Zollner describing 3% as a more comfortable level for the RBNZ to sit at. ASB expects further hikes in December and February, taking the OCR to a peak of 3.5%, and has lifted its estimate of the neutral rate, the level that neither stimulates nor restrains the economy, to around 3.5%. BNZ said the RBNZ should signal that more tightening is coming. Westpac has the most hawkish track, with hikes in December and February to 3.5%, followed by further increases in June and September 2027 to a peak of 4%. Westpac also said a split committee vote was very possible.

The drivers are oil and the currency. Higher fuel prices and a weaker New Zealand dollar have lifted the inflation outlook, and while annual inflation eased to 3.7% in the September quarter, banks expect it to climb back toward 4.5% to 4.7% by the December quarter.

Today’s meeting is a Monetary Policy Review rather than a full Monetary Policy Statement, so it will not include updated forecasts or a projected rate track. That leaves the tone of the short statement, any hint at the next move and the voting record as the main signals for markets. The decision also lands 10 days before New Zealand’s November 7 general election, although Governor Anna Breman has said the election is not a factor in policy decisions.

item.title: Bessent says SEC and CFTC can fill the Clarity Act gap, but agency rules come with an expiry risk
item.description:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says Washington can still deliver crypto rules without Congress. Speaking at Ripple’s Swell conference, he said the Senate’s failure to pass the Clarity Act was disappointing, but that Treasury would use its convening power to push a regulatory framework forward through agency action with the SEC and CFTC. The catch for investors is durability: rules written by regulators can be rewritten by the next set of regulators.

What happened

Bessent described the SEC and CFTC as “great partners” in the effort. He also raised debanking, the practice of financial institutions cutting off services to crypto businesses, sometimes allegedly under regulatory pressure. He said the Clarity Act could have prevented a repeat of that, but that regulatory best practices and protections can still reduce the risk. He also argued that stablecoins will lift demand for the US dollar and Treasuries, making them an important funding source for the government.

The backdrop is the Senate vote six weeks ago. The Clarity Act failed to advance on September 15 on a 49-50 vote, 11 short of the 60 needed. Because the vote was procedural, the bill was never debated or amended. The two disputes that sank it were ethics rules covering officials’ digital asset holdings and whether stablecoin issuers can offer yield or rewards.

Why it matters

The bill would have settled the question that has dogged US crypto for years: which regulator is responsible for which tokens. It would have given the CFTC oversight of decentralized digital commodities while leaving fundraising and investment contracts with the SEC. Without it, the agencies are building the framework piece by piece.

That work was already underway before Bessent spoke. The SEC proposed Regulation Crypto Assets on August 18, and on September 17 it launched an innovation exemption for tokenized securities venues, while the CFTC sent its crypto market rules to the White House for review. So Bessent’s comments are less a new policy than Treasury putting its weight behind the agency route, with debanking added to the agenda.

The limitation is permanence. SEC Chair Paul Atkins has himself argued that legislation is still needed for rules a future regulator cannot undo, and agency rules can also face court challenges. JPMorgan said last week that regulator actions partly offset the Clarity setback, but that political and legal risks will remain until Congress passes a market structure law, since a future administration could reverse agency actions.

What could change the interpretation

A revived bill would shift the picture quickly. JPMorgan sees the Clarity Act as unlikely to pass this year but possibly returning in 2027. In the other direction, a legal challenge to an SEC or CFTC rule would underline how fragile the agency approach is. It is also worth separating intent from action: Bessent said Treasury could work with the agencies, which is a statement of direction, not a finished rule.

What to watch next

The next concrete milestone is the CFTC’s crypto market rules emerging from White House review, followed by the SEC finalising Regulation Crypto Assets. Any Treasury guidance on debanking would be the first tangible sign that Bessent’s new thread is more than rhetoric. Next week’s US midterm elections also matter, as the make-up of the next Congress will shape whether market structure legislation has a realistic path in 2027.

For readers, the practical takeaway is to treat agency progress as useful but provisional. Clearer rules from regulators can lower near-term uncertainty for exchanges and token issuers, but until Congress acts, part of the regulatory risk premium is likely to stay in the price. Steady agency progress would strengthen the case that the Clarity failure was a delay rather than a dead end. Stalled rules or court fights would weaken it. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: UBS sees Brent near $110 by year-end, lifts 2027 forecasts on freight and supply risks
item.description:
UBS is arguing that the oil market’s tightness has moved from production to logistics. Even with Gulf flows close to pre-conflict levels, shipping attacks and scarce tankers keep delivered crude expensive, which means a supply recovery alone may not bring prices down much. With strategic reserve releases largely done and Chinese buying back, the market has lost two of its main shock absorbers, leaving it more exposed to any new disruption around Hormuz. Higher-for-longer oil also keeps inflation pressure in play ahead of the Fed decision, adding to the case for further tightening and weighing on rate-sensitive assets. Freight-sensitive refiners and importers in Asia are the most exposed to the shift from barrel scarcity to shipping scarcity.

---

Earlier:

  • Oil: Private survey of inventory shows a headline crude oil draw vs build expected

---

Gulf oil is flowing again, but UBS says record attacks on shipping, drained inventories and returning Chinese demand mean the barrels are getting more expensive to move, keeping Brent elevated well into 2027.

Summary:

  • UBS expects Brent to hold near $110 by year-end and raised its 2027 forecasts: March to $95 from $90, June to $90 from $85 and September to $85 from $80.
  • Global inventories have fallen sharply and pledged strategic reserve releases are largely complete, which UBS says should support prices.
  • Combined Hormuz and bypass pipeline flows recovered to close to 18.8 million bpd in early October, against 19.9 million before the conflict.
  • At least 30 attacks on ships near the Strait were reported in October, a monthly record, pushing freight rates higher and squeezing tanker capacity.
  • Chinese crude imports have recovered from earlier lows, removing a key shock absorber for the market.
  • Brent eased around 0.5% to around $115 on Tuesday and US crude fell to around $101, ahead of the Fed decision.

UBS expects Brent crude to hold near $110 a barrel by year-end and has raised its 2027 price forecasts, arguing that depleted inventories, record freight costs and recovering Chinese demand will keep oil elevated even as Middle Eastern supply recovers from this year’s disruption.

The bank lifted its March 2027 Brent forecast to $95 from $90, its June 2027 forecast to $90 from $85 and its September 2027 forecast to $85 from $80. The upgrades came as oil fell for a second straight session on Tuesday, with Brent easing around 0.5% to around $115 and US crude slipping around 0.4% to around $101, as investors awaited major corporate earnings and the Federal Reserve’s rate decision. Brent is still up around 91% this year and US crude around 78%.

UBS said global inventories have fallen sharply and that pledged releases from strategic oil reserves are now largely complete, removing a buffer that had helped cushion supply losses. An undersupplied market could drain commercial stocks further, which the bank said should keep prices supported.

Middle Eastern loadings have recovered substantially from the severe disruption earlier in the year. Citing data from Petro-Logistics, UBS said combined crude flows through the Strait of Hormuz and bypass pipelines were estimated at more than 17.3 million barrels per day in September and close to 18.8 million in the first three weeks of October, compared with an average of 19.9 million in January and February before the conflict.

That recovery, however, has come alongside a sharp deterioration in maritime security. At least 30 attacks on ships in and around the Strait were reported in October, the highest monthly total on record, pushing freight rates higher and limiting tanker availability. UBS said this means the oil balance now depends not only on how many barrels are produced, but on whether there is enough affordable shipping capacity to move them where they are needed. Freight sets the delivered cost of crude, and tight shipping can reshape regional trade flows and refinery economics.

Chinese buying is the final factor UBS highlighted. Imports have recovered materially from exceptional lows earlier this year, removing what had been an important shock absorber for the global market.

UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo said uncertainty around the bank’s forecasts remains high, reflecting the unpredictable course of the Middle East conflict and the pace of recovery in both Gulf production and global oil demand. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: HSBC shares slide almost 7% as revenue misses and wealth stalls despite 32% profit jump
item.description:
The sell-off shows how much was already priced into HSBC after a strong run. Without a guidance upgrade, a revenue miss and stalled wealth growth were enough to trigger profit-taking. The read-across for Hong Kong and Asian banks is margin pressure: costlier time deposits threaten interest income just as the Fed’s hiking path keeps funding costs high. Oil matters indirectly, since inflation and rate uncertainty linked to the Iran war is weighing on bank valuations broadly, and HSBC is already setting aside provisions for the Middle East conflict. The Basel 3.1 capital boost from January 2027 gives HSBC room to expand buybacks, which could limit further downside once the disappointment fades.

---

Earlier:

  • Goldman: Markets selling US banks on higher rates, but income guidance rises into 2027

--- HSBC delivered a big profit jump and another $1 billion buyback, but a revenue miss, flat wealth income and no upgrade to its targets were enough to send the shares sharply lower.

Summary:

  • HSBC shares fell almost 7% on Tuesday after third-quarter revenue of around $18.6 billion missed forecasts of roughly $19.1 billion, and adjusted EPS of $2.10 missed $2.22.
  • Pre-tax profit rose 32% to around $9.6 billion, helped by the absence of last year’s legal provisions. Excluding notable items, it rose about 10% to around $10 billion.
  • Wealth revenue was flat at around $2.7 billion after strong growth in the first half. Net interest income rose 6% but was slightly below expectations.
  • Deposit competition in Hong Kong and the UK is rising, with time deposits at 38% of the Hong Kong mix.
  • Guidance was reaffirmed, not raised: banking NII of at least $46 billion in 2026 and a RoTE of at least 17% for 2026 to 2028.
  • HSBC announced a new buyback of up to $1 billion. CET1 eased to 13.9%, with Basel 3.1 expected to add 40 to 50bp from January 2027.

HSBC shares fell almost 7% on Tuesday after third-quarter revenue missed forecasts and its wealth business stalled, overshadowing a 32% jump in pre-tax profit to around $9.6 billion and a fresh buyback of up to $1 billion.

Revenue came in at around $18.6 billion for the July to September quarter, short of the roughly $19.1 billion analysts had expected, while adjusted earnings per share of $2.10 missed the $2.22 consensus. Pre-tax profit was broadly in line with estimates, but the headline gain was flattered by the absence of legal provisions booked a year earlier. Excluding notable items, profit rose about 10% to around $10 billion.

The weakest spot was wealth, one of the bank’s main growth engines. Wealth revenue was flat at around $2.7 billion, after year-on-year growth of 15% and 23% in the first two quarters, although net new money in Asia remained strong at around $38 billion for the quarter. Net interest income rose 6% to around $9.3 billion, slightly below expectations, with the net interest margin, the gap between what the bank earns on loans and pays on deposits, steady at 1.57%.

Analysts flagged rising competition for deposits in Hong Kong and the UK as a pressure point. Time deposits, which pay savers higher rates, rose to 38% of HSBC’s Hong Kong deposit mix, a shift that tends to erode margins. Management said deposit competition in Hong Kong was the bigger factor for interest income.

Investors had also hoped for upgrades. HSBC reaffirmed, rather than raised, its guidance for banking net interest income of at least $46 billion this year and a return on tangible equity of at least 17% from 2026 to 2028, with revenue growth reaching 5% by 2028. Chief financial officer Pam Kaur acknowledged that the market sometimes expects guidance or targets to be lifted.

Credit quality held up. Expected credit losses fell 17% to around $800 million, helped by lower charges on Hong Kong commercial real estate, while the bank’s nine-month provisions include allowances for uncertainty linked to the Middle East conflict. The CET1 capital ratio slipped to 13.9%. HSBC expects incoming Basel 3.1 rules to add 40 to 50 basis points to that ratio from January 2027, against a 14% to 14.5% target range, and said buybacks remain its preferred way to return surplus capital.

The reaction leaves HSBC needing to show that wealth momentum can recover and that deposit costs will not eat further into margins when it reports full-year results.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Standard Chartered: Gold must hold $3,886 or risk deeper correction as oil fuels hike bets
item.description:
Oil is the key driver here: Standard Chartered’s warning ties gold’s next move directly to crude, with each leg higher in oil feeding inflation and Fed hike expectations, a pressure gold has struggled to withstand. With a December hike largely priced, any hawkish tone from the Fed on Wednesday could push gold toward the $3,886 support. A break there could trigger further liquidation from underwater ETP holders. On the other side, positioning is at its lightest since May and short covering has started, which leaves room for a sharp rebound if oil eases or the dollar softens. Physical buying around Diwali is a near-term test of whether Asian demand can step in where Western investors have pulled back.

-

Standard Chartered still sees gold higher by early next year, but says it first needs to find a floor while rising oil keeps the Fed in hiking mode.

Summary:

  • Standard Chartered says gold must hold $3,886 support after falling below $4,000, warning that a sustained break could bring a much deeper correction.
  • Higher oil prices are keeping inflation risks and Fed tightening expectations in focus. Markets price under a 10% chance of a hike this week and around 86% odds in December.
  • The 10-year Treasury yield has eased to just under 5%, but this has given gold little support, and the dollar remains a major headwind.
  • Gold ETPs saw renewed outflows late last week, and at least 350 tonnes of ETP holdings are now in loss-making territory. Speculative positioning is at its lowest since May after eight weeks of cuts.
  • Indian imports fell 83% in September, but Diwali on November 8 could revive buying. Chinese imports rose 34% to around 145 tonnes.
  • The bank kept its forecasts for gold to average $4,650 in Q4 and $4,850 in Q1 2027.

Gold needs to establish a floor after slipping below $4,000 an ounce, or risks a much deeper correction, Standard Chartered warned, with higher oil prices keeping inflation risks and further Federal Reserve tightening in focus, according to the bank’s latest precious metals report as reported by Kitco.

Suki Cooper, Standard Chartered’s global head of commodities research, said gold needs to hold support at $3,886. A sustained break below that level could expose the market to a significantly larger decline, even though a two-month downtrend has pushed prices close to oversold territory. Cooper said elevated energy prices continue to push inflation pressure higher, forcing investors to reassess the outlook for US monetary policy and weighing on the metal.

Standard Chartered said markets see less than a 10% chance of a Fed rate hike at Wednesday’s meeting but price around 86% odds of a move in December, after the US midterm elections. The 10-year Treasury yield has eased to just under 5% from around 5.3% earlier this month, but Cooper said the drop has done little for gold, with investors focused on persistent inflation and the risk of more tightening. The US dollar remains a major headwind, with gold’s three-month rolling correlation with the greenback at minus 47%.

Investment demand has softened. Global gold-backed exchange-traded products, or ETPs, saw renewed outflows late last week, with holdings down 1.3 tonnes, although October flows remain marginally positive. Cooper said the sell-off extended across asset classes, reflecting technology-sector jitters and investors raising cash to meet margin calls. She estimated that at least 350 tonnes of ETP holdings are now in loss-making territory at current prices, which could leave the market vulnerable to further liquidation.

Positioning, however, may be nearing a turning point. Speculative investors have cut their gold exposure for eight straight weeks, taking positioning to its lowest level since May, and Cooper said some short covering suggests speculators may be starting to look for a floor.

Asian physical demand could also offer support. Indian imports fell 83% year on year in September to around 14 tonnes, the weakest monthly level since January 2023, as a weak monsoon and high prices delayed seasonal buying. Cooper said demand could pick up ahead of the Diwali festival on November 8 as retailers restock. Chinese imports rose 34% to around 145 tonnes in September, taking the year-to-date total to around 1,290 tonnes, up 67%.

Despite the near-term risks, the bank kept its forecasts for gold to average $4,650 in the fourth quarter and $4,850 in the first quarter of 2027, noting that central banks and ETP investors have generally treated price corrections as buying opportunities this year. Cooper cautioned that the coming weeks could stay volatile, with gold likely to keep testing its floor if oil prices extend their gains and keep inflation expectations elevated.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman: Markets selling US banks on higher rates, but income guidance rises into 2027
item.description:
Goldman’s view puts bank stocks at the centre of the debate over higher-for-longer rates: with the Fed still on a hiking path, unrealised bond losses are keeping investors away despite improving income guidance. If yields stabilise, or the regulatory changes Goldman flags make 2027 buybacks more likely, the gap between earnings and share prices could narrow quickly. Deposits pooling in the largest lenders point to more pressure on regional and smaller bank funding costs. The credit team’s preference for secured, collateral-backed lending over unsecured bonds is a cautious signal for the heavy pipeline of AI-related bond supply.

---

Earlier:

  • ICYMI: S&P sees global bond issuance growth slowing to 2.7% in 2027, weakest in five years

---

Goldman says US banks are being sold for what higher rates do to their bond portfolios, not for what those rates are doing to their earnings, and it thinks the gap is the opportunity.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs says around 80% of early-reporting S&P 500 companies beat Q3 earnings estimates, but market reactions have been muted as higher yields shift the focus to margin durability, earnings quality and 2027 guidance.
  • US banks reported robust fundamentals: net interest income guidance extended into 2027, equity trading surged and credit metrics stayed benign.
  • Bank shares still fell. Goldman says investors are focused on capital pressure from unrealised bond losses, which it sees as largely a timing issue, with regulatory changes possibly supporting buybacks in 2027.
  • Several bank CEOs flagged a once-in-a-generation capital shortage to fund the AI boom, while rejecting third-party agentic AI transacting on client accounts on security grounds.
  • Goldman’s credit team prefers secured, amortising loans against collateral and contracts over unsecured bonds.
  • The top 10 US banks captured around 85% of Q3 deposit growth, with one bank taking around 30%. Consumer activity and credit trends remain broadly healthy.

Goldman Sachs says US bank shares have been punished despite strong third-quarter results, arguing that investors are trading on a single idea, that higher rates mean selling financials, while overlooking guidance for rising interest income into 2027, according to a third-quarter earnings review from the firm.

Corporate results have been resilient overall. Goldman said roughly 80% of the early-reporting S&P 500 companies beat earnings estimates, but equity market reactions to those beats have been muted. With investors weighing the impact of higher yields, the focus has moved away from headline quarterly beats toward how durable margins are, the quality of earnings and whether forward guidance through 2027 is credible.

Banks, typically among the first to report, delivered solid numbers. Goldman said guidance for net interest income, the gap between what banks earn on loans and securities and what they pay on deposits, was extended into 2027 as fixed-rate assets reprice at higher yields. Equity trading revenue surged and credit metrics remained benign.

The bank argues that the market’s response reflects the two-sided effect of higher rates. Rising rates lift interest income but also weigh on capital through unrealised losses on bond portfolios, and Goldman believes that capital side is where investor attention is concentrated. It sees the gap between those two effects as the potential opportunity, describing capital pressure as largely a matter of timing and noting that upcoming regulatory changes could support share buybacks in 2027. Most banks that provided guidance expect interest income and net interest margins to keep rising into 2027.

AI featured prominently in bank commentary. Several chief executives warned of a once-in-a-generation capital shortage to fund the AI boom, while also rejecting third-party agentic AI, meaning autonomous software agents, carrying out transactions on client accounts because of security concerns, even as their own internal AI tools scaled rapidly. Goldman’s credit team sees a similar divide in AI more broadly, with demand intact but access to funding now separating winners from the rest. The team remains cautious, favouring secured, amortising loans backed by collateral and contracts over unsecured bonds.

Concentration in the sector is also rising. Goldman said the 10 largest US banks captured roughly 85% of third-quarter deposit growth, and a single bank took around 30%, leaving little for the more than 4,200 remaining institutions.

On consumers, Goldman’s consumer sector analyst Cecile Origenes said pressure at lower income levels has not translated into broad deterioration, and that the more important question as earnings season continues is where consumers are still prepared to spend and which companies can capture that demand without sacrificing margins. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

AI borrowing stays the main swing factor for supply: with capex expected to top $1.3 trillion, hyperscaler issuance will keep testing investor appetite for technology credit. The reference to the Middle East war links the outlook to oil. Any renewed rise in crude would feed inflation, push back hopes of lower rates and strengthen the headwinds S&P describes. A growing share of Chinese debt in global benchmarks would also gradually leave index-tracking funds more exposed to Chinese rate moves.

---

After a bumper 2026, S&P expects growth in global bond issuance to slow to a crawl next year, though AI borrowing and refinancing needs mean the debt keeps coming.

Summary:

  • S&P Global Ratings forecasts global bond issuance growth of 2.7% in 2027, down from an estimated 12.2% in 2026 and the slowest pace in five years.
  • Total global issuance is expected to reach around $11.7 trillion this year.
  • Higher interest rates and uncertainty linked to the Middle East war could curb borrowers’ appetite.
  • Hyperscaler bond issuance is nearing $300 billion this year and is expected to rise more slowly in 2027, with AI-related capex forecast to top $1.3 trillion.
  • China is likely to remain a source of issuance growth as falling government bond yields lower borrowing costs.
  • Demand for sovereign and corporate debt remains robust, and corporate bond spreads have narrowed.

Growth in global bond issuance is set to slow sharply next year, with S&P Global Ratings forecasting a 2.7% increase in 2027, down from an estimated 12.2% this year and the weakest pace in five years, according to reports of its latest outlook published Tuesday.

The slowdown comes off a very high base. S&P expects total global issuance to reach around $11.7 trillion in 2026, so even modest growth next year would keep volumes at very large levels. The forecast points to a loss of momentum rather than a retreat by borrowers from debt markets.

Two factors could hold issuers back, according to S&P. Interest rates remain elevated, raising the cost of new borrowing and of refinancing existing debt, and uncertainty linked to the Middle East war could make some borrowers more cautious about timing. Many issuers have limited room to wait, however, with maturing corporate debt needing to be refinanced and governments continuing to borrow to cover defence spending and the costs of ageing populations.

Artificial intelligence remains one of the main sources of supply. Bond issuance by hyperscalers, the large cloud and data centre operators financing AI infrastructure, is approaching $300 billion this year, and S&P expects it to rise again in 2027, though at a slower pace. AI-related capital expenditure is forecast to exceed $1.3 trillion next year, which suggests the largest technology companies will keep returning to debt markets to fund it.

China is expected to remain a source of growth. Falling Chinese government bond yields have lowered borrowing costs for local issuers, and continued growth in issuance there could gradually lift China’s weight in major bond benchmarks. That would increase the exposure of index-tracking funds to Chinese interest rate moves and to currency hedging decisions.

Demand has so far kept pace with supply. S&P said appetite for sovereign and corporate debt remains robust, and corporate bond spreads, the extra yield investors demand over government debt, have narrowed, indicating that investors have absorbed this year’s heavy issuance without requiring much additional compensation.

The 2027 outlook therefore hinges less on investor demand than on the cost of borrowing. If rates stay high and geopolitical uncertainty persists, issuance growth could stay subdued beyond next year.

item.title: ICYMI: Fitch sees Fed hiking to 4.25% in December, says US credit outlook still benign
item.description:
Fitch’s December call fits the view that the Fed is still on a hiking path, which supports front-end Treasury yields and the US dollar and argues against any near-term easing. The more telling signal for credit is the split it describes: investment-grade spreads near multi-year lows while CCC yields have blown out. Heavy hyperscaler issuance on top of Treasury supply raises the risk that new deals need bigger concessions even where credit quality holds up. For equities, putting a recession scenario next to AI capex keeps the spotlight on any sign that hyperscalers are scaling back spending plans.

---

I spotted the headlines from Fitch overngiht and just bringing it to investingLive now. Fitch trails behind S&P and Moody's but I doubt their analysis and conclusions would be too much different. 

----

Fitch still calls US credit benign overall, but its December Fed hike call, record private credit defaults and an AI-driven recession scenario show the pressure building on the weakest borrowers.

Summary:

  • Fitch expects the US credit outlook to stay broadly benign, though higher-for-longer rates and AI funding needs will test interest-sensitive and lower-rated borrowers.
  • It raised its US GDP forecasts for 2026 and 2027 by 0.2 point to 2.1% each, and expects the Fed to hike to 4.25% in December and hold through 2027.
  • US fixed-income issuance rose around 10% year on year in the first nine months, and corporate bond issuance rose around 25%, driven partly by hyperscaler AI borrowing.
  • Investment-grade spreads remain near multi-year lows, while CCC yields have widened by about 480 basis points this year.
  • Fitch calls AI both the main growth driver and a key downside risk. Its adverse AI equity-correction scenario would mean a US recession, with GDP falling 0.6% in 2027.
  • Fitch’s private credit default rate hit a record 6.3% in the 12 months to September, and leveraged loan defaults are expected near the low end of its 4.5% to 5.0% year-end range.

Fitch Ratings expects the US credit outlook to remain broadly benign, even as higher-for-longer interest rates and rising AI-related funding needs put interest-sensitive and lower-rated borrowers under pressure, according to a Fitch Wire commentary published Tuesday alongside its fourth-quarter US credit brief.

The ratings agency has lifted its US growth forecasts for both 2026 and 2027 by 0.2 percentage point to 2.1%, pointing to resilient consumer spending and AI-driven private investment. Fixed investment is forecast to grow 4.8% this year and 4.6% next year. On policy, Fitch expects the Federal Reserve to raise its policy rate to 4.25% in December and keep it there through 2027, which it says will sustain pressure on borrowers who need to refinance at higher costs.

Funding conditions are also being shaped by heavy Treasury supply and increased borrowing by hyperscalers, the large cloud and data centre operators, to pay for AI capital spending. Fitch said US fixed-income issuance rose around 10% year on year in the first nine months of 2026, while corporate bond issuance climbed around 25%. The picture across the credit spectrum is uneven. Investment-grade spreads remain near multi-year lows, while yields on CCC-rated debt, the lowest rung of high yield, have widened by about 480 basis points since the start of the year.

Fitch described AI investment as both the main growth driver and a key downside risk. IT-related private investment grew around 18% year on year in the second quarter, but the agency warned that intensifying competition and cheaper open-weight models could weaken the pricing power of AI service providers and prompt a rethink of hyperscaler capex plans over the next one to three years. Under Fitch’s adverse AI equity-correction scenario, the US would fall into recession, with GDP contracting 0.6% in 2027. Its sector-level AI stress test found broad resilience, with material risks concentrated in services, data centres, and telecommunications, media and technology.

Higher rates are weighing most heavily on housing-related sectors and lower-rated borrowers. Fitch’s US private credit default rate reached a record 6.3% in the 12 months to September, and the agency expects leveraged loan defaults to rise toward the low end of its 4.5% to 5.0% year-end forecast range.

The commentary leaves the Fed’s December decision and the durability of AI spending as the two variables most likely to determine whether a benign outlook for credit overall holds up for its weakest borrowers. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
